title: 'The race will be wide open' – With no long climbs and no individual time trial, does the 2027 Tour de France Femmes route suit home favourite Pauline Ferrand-Prévot?
author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
text:
Two summers ago, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot soared to a historic home victory at the Tour de France Femmes, dominating the closing Alpine stages to deliver a first French Tour win in decades and the biggest win of her career.

She beat Demi Vollering by almost four minutes in Châtel, but this year the tables turned as Ferrand-Prévot endured a disastrous title defence , losing minutes in the Dijon time trial before falling out of contention in the Ardèche hills and conceding defeat on Mont Ventoux.

Clearly, a rider of Ferrand-Prévot's calibre is better than her early-August performance, and the Visma-Lease a Bike star will aim to bounce back next year. But is the 2027 Tour de France Femmes route one where she can thrive and take back the yellow jersey from Vollering?

Well, race director Marion Rousse delivered both good and bad news for the 34-year-old and her team in the Palais des Congrès in Paris on Thursday afternoon.

For a start, there's no individual time trial on next year's route. That will be music to Ferrand-Prévot's ears after she lost two minutes to Vollering and Marlen Reusser over just 21km on the road to Dijon in August.

Ferrand-Prévot was always expected to shed time against the clock, even as her team protested how much she had trained on the TT bike, so for a start, she's already looking at several minutes saved. Coming in place of an individual time trial, however, is a team test in the form of a flat 18km tour of central London.

Team time trials are rare in women's cycling, with next year's stage a first in Tour de France Femmes history. The other Grand Tours have featured a TTT in recent history, though, with the Giro featuring one in 2021 and the Vuelta doing so between 2022 and 2025.

Do Visma have the personnel to succeed in such a test? Time will tell, and it's impossible to make any predictions this far out, but in former time trial specialist Jos van Emden , they have a directeur sportif well-placed to guide them in London.

"The team time trial is a notable feature. It’s an event we haven't seen before in the Tour de France Femmes," Van Emden said after the route unveiling.

"I'm a fan of team time trials. We haven't raced many of them as a team, so it's difficult to make any immediate predictions about our collective strength or the course in London. You have to master every discipline if you want to win the Tour. This will be another new challenge.

"That decision shows that women's cycling is continuing to evolve and grow in importance. A team time trial is part of what makes the Tour the Tour, as it’s the biggest stage in cycling."

Is there enough climbing for PFP?

The goal will likely be to limit losses and keep Ferrand-Prévot close to her main yellow jersey rivals as the race hits France, with the opening two stages in the north of England unlikely to have produced much in the way of GC gaps.

On the mainland, it will all be about surviving the pitfalls of the sprint stages and then overcoming the tricky, punchy hills on the road to Magnanville on stage 5.

The big time differences, however, should be made in the final three days as the race reaches the Massif Central, though there are no long Alpine climbs on the menu here like the Madeleine, where Ferrand-Prévot built her 2025 Tour victory with that dominant solo ride.

Will that be a problem for the lightweight climber?

"The first thing that stands out to me is how different this Tour is from the editions in recent years. The high mountains are missing. That was certainly different in previous editions," Van Emden said.

Stage 7 features a closing climb to La Loge des Gardes (6.7km at 7.1%), while the mid-mountain stage 8 to Clermont-Ferrand features the Côte de Charade (6km at 5.9%) before a descent to the finish. The showpiece final stage concludes atop the Puy de Dôme , which measures 11.3km at an average gradient of 7.8%.

Van Emden said that the Tour is no easier than the recent editions, even if the Puy de Dôme stage doesn't quite measure up to the recent queen stages of the Glandon-Alpe d'Huez in 2024, the Madeleine last year, or the Ventoux in August.

"The longest climb in this Tour is 11km. That was different in recent years. But that doesn’t mean this will be an easier Tour," he said.

"Quite the opposite: the race will be wide open, and the general classification contenders will be fighting for every second in every stage.

"That’s a very special way to finish. In cycling, this climb may not be as well known as Mont Ventoux or the Col de la Madeleine, which featured in recent editions, but that’s also because it’s a protected natural area. I’m really looking forward to finishing atop the volcano."

As is the case for the men's race, there's clearly one standout favourite for next year's Tour de France Femmes – the defending champion. This Tour route certainly isn't built with Ferrand-Prévot in mind, but success isn't out of reach, and if she's back on form, next August could well host the Ferrand-Prévot vs Vollering battle we've been waiting for.

Between now and then, there's plenty of time for training, planning, and recon rides. The planning will get underway soon, said Van Emden.

"We’ll draw up our plans this winter. With Pauline, we have the 2025 Tour winner on our team, although she would normally be better suited to the longer climbs.

"But we have several cards to play. I think this route suits us very well. It’s going to be an explosive Tour."

title: The young Americans choosing Y2K cars over shiny new SUVs: ‘I get so much crap from people’
author: Andrew Lawrence and photographs by Jordan Putt in Kennesaw, Georgia
text:
People under 35 are hunting for no-frills rides they can pay for in cash and fix themselves – defying expectations to take on steep loans

J ack Price joined the Marines in fall 2021 knowing he would need a car to get around base and that he couldn’t afford a new one. A joyless, month-long search through dealer classifieds and Facebook Marketplace listings ended when his mother spotted a 2010 Volkswagen Jetta posted on her office listserv by a co-worker moving abroad. With just 60,000 miles (96,560km) on themeter, the car (a manual!) was mechanically sound, and the air conditioning, sunroof and Bluetooth radio worked too. At $6,000, it was a steal. Price paid in cash.

Five years on, the Jetta, which he called the Pewter Pebble, is still carting him from A to B in unassuming style. “I’ve completely driven it into the ground,” says the 30-year-old, who lives in Los Angeles. “All over bases, cross-country a couple times, not really lovingly. I get so much crap from people, but not people my age.”

For generations, buying a first new car has been a rite of passage in the US, the clearest sign of a young person responsibly striking out on their own. But younger millennials and gen Z are increasingly finding that path blocked. The average new vehicle costs more than $50,000, an alarming figure that reflects Americans’ insatiable appetite for progressively larger SUVs and pickups. Meanwhile, adults under 35 are disappearing from showroom floors, accounting for less than 10% of new vehicle registrations in 2024 – a new low.

According to the credit reporting agency Experian, the average monthly car payment in the US is $765 for a new car and $542 for a used one, with the loan terms now stretching to six, even seven, years. A record 21% of new-car buyers pay $1,000 or more a month , according to the autos research group Edmunds. And that’s before factoring in maintenance, fluctuating gas prices and the eye-watering insurance premiums often charged to drivers under 35.

For many young Americans already under the strain of student loans, high housing costs and an unforgiving labor market, buying a new car or even a newer used one is out of the question. Enter the Y2K car – the retro ride that has become a trendy romantic choice for some younger Americans. “There’s definitely a golden era of cars from the late 90s and early 2000s that people just really want all of a sudden,” says Charlie Spears, a service adviser at an independently owned repair shop in Atlanta who conducts prepurchase inspections of used cars on demand. “A lot of people just want something that’s not going to fail them.”

Y2K cars don’t encompass everything produced in that era. They are the ones that simply won’t die. Think wedge-shaped Honda Accords and slab-sided Toyota Camrys: dependable, hand-me-down transport that can last 150,000 miles or more with routine maintenance. (Price’s Jetta, which was built at the end of a model production run that began in 2005, just makes the cut.) They’re economical to run and relatively inexpensive to insure, owing to their drastically lower worth. Best of all, the purchase price is low enough to pay in cash. Even when buyers need a loan – at steep interest rates as modern cars have in effect become mortgage payments on wheels – they can pay it off in a fraction of the time it takes to finance a newer car.

The supply of these bargains is dwindling: used vehicles priced under $15,000, the sweet spot for Y2K cars, have shrunk from 21% of inventory a year ago to 15% , according to industry analysis from Cox Automotive – numbers that speak to the demand for affordable cars. “Part of the draw is the nostalgia factor – people wanting cars they grew up with,” says Consumer Reports’ autos expert Keith Barry. “An old car with the right music on is kind of the closest thing to a time machine.”

On social media, the Y2K car has emerged as an ironic status symbol – a marker of maturity, grit and lack of pretense. Defects – busted aircon, glitchy windows, bits and bobs that have failed, fallen off or been held on with gaffer tape – are simply treated as part of a Y2K car’s personality. “I don’t know what kind of disease that is in the brain,” says one TikTok creator, who has to pry open the fuel door of her 2003 Mitsubishi Outlander with a screwdriver . “But I don’t get frustrated. I’m like, ‘Oh, this is fun.’”

In a Y2K car that takes a lickin’ and keeps on tickin’, creature comforts are beside the point. For many, part of the appeal is the absence of dashboard infotainment displays and other screens that have replaced basic switches and knobs in newer cars, often in the name of cost-cutting. Automakers’ zeal to monetize in-car technology, sometimes charging extra to activate physically installed features such as heated seats and remote start, only reinforces young buyers’ doubts about the value of a new car.

At the same time, do-it-yourself repairs have become harder as cars grow more digitally complex and auto manufacturers cut off access to owners and even independent mechanics . Oftentimes, they require investing in specialty digital readers or computer software to diagnose problems, and bespoke tools for wrenching. Most car owners would sooner punt, take the car to the dealership and pay whatever the maintenance and repair costs – which, of course, is exactly the vertical integration that shareholder-bound manufacturers are after.

Hence the romance with Y2K cars: you can fix ‘em yourself, their old-school controls fall easily to hand, they’re tried and tested, seemingly built to last. They just have an aura of invincibility – never mind that their age makes them fundamentally more dangerous and susceptible to frequent repairs. “I’ve used my Jetta as if it were a truck,” Price says. “Transported trees in it, put my surfboard through the sunroof. I’ve done every single thing possible to thrash it beyond its abilities.”…

title: Ukraine learns to fight without Starlink as Musk plays politics with satellites
author: Jeremy Hsu
text:
Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service has played a pivotal role in supporting Ukraine’s successful resistance to Russia’s full-scale invasion for years. But with Starlink having become increasingly unreliable due to Musk’s political inclinations and the latest surprise disruptions to service in Ukraine, the Ukrainians and Europe as a whole are now facing urgent questions about how to move forward without it.

As the world’s largest communications satellite network, Starlink can typically support high-speed Internet and data streams for any user or vehicle equipped with a relatively compact Starlink terminal. This has enabled Ukraine to maintain vital communications for both civilian purposes and military operations—and has also expanded the Ukrainian military’s capability to remotely control or provide guidance to drones used in both air defense against Russian attacks and for striking back at Russian targets.

“Starlink currently offers some of the best satellite coverage available, with virtually no competitors when you consider the combination of cost, availability, and ease of use,” according to the head of hardware R&D at the Ukrainian defense company BlueBird Tech , who provided comments to Ars anonymously for security reasons. “In practical terms, the main limitation is the need to position the antenna so it can receive signals from the satellites.”

title: Former Man United chief Murtough joins Birmingham
text:
Birmingham City have appointed former Manchester United chief John Murtough as their new director of football.

Murtough, 55, who left United in April 2024 as football director after 11 years at Old Trafford, becomes the replacement for Craig Gardner, who departed St Andrew's in June.

Murtough, who has also worked for Everton, Fulham and Coventry City, was with the Premier League before joining Manchester United in 2013.

His most recent role was in Serie A as director of global development at Atalanta.

Murtough will begin his role at US-owned Birmingham on Monday - following this weekend's Championship game at Cardiff City.

Blues currently sit fourth in the Championship after a run of three straight wins since the international break under head coach Chris Davies.

Birmingham Sports Quarter - what you need to know

In a statement, Birmingham have said Davies "will report into" Murtough, who will report directly into the Blues board.

Murtough will also "collaborate with Hope Powell to ensure that the Blues women's team, enjoy "continued development benefits from the club's wider football strategy".

Blues, twice Women's Super League runners-up in 2011 and 2012, currently sit 13th, one place off the bottom, in the table.

"This is a great football club with brilliant fans and enormous potential" said Murtough. "There is a clear determination from Knighthead to build something special for the long term, both on and off the pitch."

In a board statement, owners Knighthead Capital Management said: "We have been clear from the outset about our ambition for this club and for the city of Birmingham.

"We want Birmingham City competing at the highest level of English football and we are building for sustained success, both on and off the pitch."

Murtough began his career working alongside David Moyes at Everton as a sports scientist, working his way up to become head of performance before leaving in 2012 to become Premier League head of elite performance.

He then joined Man United in 2013, going on to become head of football development, before being promoted to football director in March 2020 a role that gave him "overall leadership and responsibility for operations and strategy across all football functions".

He was at the helm in an era that brought the sacking of Ole Gunnar Solksjaer , the short-term appointments of Michael Carrick and then Ralf Rangnick , before the unveiling of Erik ten Hag . But he had left before ten Hag was sacked in October 2024 .

Jadon Sancho , for £73m, Anthony, the second-most expensive player in the club's history when he signed from Ajax for £81.3m, Rasmus Hojlund for £72m and Mason Mount , for £55m, were all recruited under his watch.

title: Review: Crystal Lake suffers a bit from its obsession with Pam Voorhees
author: Ashley Belanger
text:
Peacock series doesn’t feel like a movie when you first press play, even though it’s set up to be a prequel to the original film. (This review includes spoilers of the original movie but avoids major spoilers.)

Instead, strives to build a drama that’s half homage, half uncharted territory, while giving a long-awaited backstory to Pamela Voorhees. The original villain in the first film, Pam Voorhees, shocked audiences in 1980 by popping up out of nowhere in the midst of a brutal camp counselor killing spree, then confronting the final girl with a Norman Bates-like delivery of the movie’s chilling tagline, “Kill her, mommy,” using the voice of her drowned son, Jason.

Although the hockey-masked killer, Jason Voorhees, became the horror icon at the center of the franchise, his mom, Pam, continued to fascinate fans, who knew very little about her. Beheaded in the first film after just 13 minutes onscreen, her spirit would occasionally appear in later films, but the original actor, Betsy Palmer, who portrayed Pam refused to return, largely because the character has no depth.

title: 'It's a question of resetting the balance' – Tour de France boss namechecks Bradley Wiggins and Federico Bahamontes to explain major increase in time trialling on 2027 route
author: Alasdair Fotheringham
text:
Tour de France director Christian Prudhomme delved deep into the race's own history books to explain exactly why organisers have opted in 2027 to make the biggest increase in time trialling in the route in 15 years

Instead, Prudhomme cited time trialling star Bradley Wiggins, who conquered Britain's first Tour de France in 2012, and the rider voted the race's greatest ever climber, 1959 winner Federico Martín Bahamontes, to explain the TT increase.

Rather than looking back at just the last three editions of the race, where Tadej Pogačar has effectively made the battle for the yellow jersey a one-man show, Prudhomme used a much bigger context to explain what provides the chance – though it's far from guaranteed – for a radical switch in the balance of power between TT specialists and climbers

"The reason is simple, although we should put things into perspective, given we're in a world where people don't put things into perspective anymore," Prudhomme told reporters at the presentation, which revealed there'll be a 38-kilometre time trial on stage 7 and a 33-kilometre TT on stage 11.

"It's been 15 years since we've had so much time trialling, during the Tour won by Bradley Wiggins, and this is done with that in mind.

"Since then the riders who won in the time trials have also won in the mountains so it made no sense to extend the TT distances because the same people won, anyway.

"But now that's not the case, we've got different kinds of riders. It's just like back in the very distant era when Federico Bahamontes took time [in the mountains] on Jacques Anquetil," a renowned time trialling specialist.

"Now it's Remco Evenepoel who gains time against the clock, which he may lose in the mountains."

"It's not anti-Tadej Pogačar"

Prudhomme's comments about Bahamontes and Anquetil regarding balance could also have referred to the 1959 Tour, won by the Eagle of Toledo in part thanks to his crushing domination in a mountain time trial on the Puy de Dôme, where riders like Anquetil were pushed to nearly four minutes back. That said, Anquetil then regained more than five on Bahamontes in the race's final TT to Dijon, a massive 69 kilometres long. But there was some kind of balance, even if Bahamontes had done more than enough to win the Tour outright by that point.

In either case, Prudhomme argued, if Evenepoel was an example for now, it wasn't simply designed to favour one rider in particular. Rather, the question of having a much higher number of time trialling kilometres in 2027 was mainly to ensure that rather than any rider gaining too much of an advantage early on, the suspense could be maintained as long as possible.

"It's a question of resetting the balance, not for the organisers but all the fans who want there to be a fight right the way to the end," Prudhomme explained.

"It's not anti-Tadej Pogačar, you put pavé or time trials or climbs in front of him, he can take time and then he gains even more time on his rivals on the descents," he added, in reference to what Pogačar did on the descent of the Tourmalet on stage 6 last July, doubling his advantage over Jonas Vingegaard after dropping him close to the summit and all but winning the Tour in the process.

"If he [Pogačar] is stronger, he's stronger," Prudhomme added. "But there is a will to rebalance things, not for a single rider in particular, just like a few years ago we tried to make the route have a more punchy kind of course to try to boost the chances of a spectacular race.

"But in any case," Prudhomme concluded, making a wordplay on an old proverb, "the organisers propose and the riders dispose. That's always true."

"There are a lot of really tough unknown or semi-unknown climbs in this Tour"

While the increase in time trialling kilometres represented one big change in route trends, Prudhomme argued that the fans should not take it for granted that the mountains in the 2027 race would be a straightforward re-run of other years.

"I hope that people will be surprised, first on paper, then after being surprised on paper, in reality. Because there are a lot of really tough unknown or semi-unknown climbs in this Tour, and others which have been around but which don't have as fearsome a reputation as they deserve," he told reporters.

"So it's true we've got some classic climbs like the Tourmalet. But I'm thinking especially of the return of the Col de Burdincurutcheta, which is one of the hardest in the French Basque Country," he said of the early climb on stage 19, 8.7km long with average gradients of 9.3%.

"Then the Col du Pré, which is really daunting, too," he added of the Alpine climb, measuring 12.6km at 7.8%, which appears before the final ascent of Saisies on stage 11.

"Then there is the stage across the Massif Central with more than 3,800 metres of vertical climbing through beautiful but tough landscapes.

"Don't forget, too, that in the first week we're in Wales, there are climbs that are really hard, right from the gun on stage 3. I know the local people there are very proud of what will be on show in their part of the world that day."

One unusual feature of the Tour de France is its mini-homage to the 2027 UCI Cycling World Championships, the so-called 'Super Worlds', which will take place on the road in the northern Alps in late August and on the track in the Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines velodrome near Paris.

Stage 10 will feature the circuit of the Côte de Domancy and finishes in Sallanches, where the road World Championships also took place in 1980 and will do again in 2027, whilst stage 21 starts in Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines and will go past the velodrome en route to the Champs-Élysées.

"We weren't going ever to do the World Championships before the World Championships actually took place, which is why there will only be two ascents of the Domancy and not 20," Prudhomme explained, "but that's where Bernard Hinault, a legend of the Tour, won the Worlds in 1980, so it's also to honour him."

"The climbs there aren't very high up, but the slopes are something special: short but really, really tough. So there will be lots to see that day, too."

And perhaps, too, in the time trials as well.

title: Retail sales in Great Britain fall as struggling households cut back
author: Mark Sweney
text:
Latest negative economic update comes as John Healey prepares to announce budget next week

Retail sales in Great Britain fell more steeply than expected last month, the latest negative economic update before the chancellor, John Healey , announces his budget next week.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the volume of goods sold fell 0.4% month on month in September, much steeper than economists’ consensus expectations of a 0.1% fall.

The decrease, which was fuelled in part by poor online sales of autumn and winter wear because of an unseasonably warm September, comes as figures show consumer confidence in the UK has fallen at the fastest rate since the Covid pandemic .

While retail sales dropped across almost all sectors of the industry, the volume of motor fuel sold soared 2.2% month on month despite prices at the pump hitting record highs, returning to levels last seen before the start of the conflict in the Middle East.

In value terms, the 6.1% increase in fuel sales was the biggest month-on-month increase since 10.9% was recorded in March, the month immediately after the start of the US-Iran conflict.

Stripping out the increase from fuel, retail sales fell 0.7% in September, much worse than the 0.1% fall forecast by the City.

“October’s sharp fall in consumer confidence and the dip in retail sales volumes in September show that times are getting tougher for households just as the all-important festive period for retailers is just around the corner,” said Paul Dales, the chief UK economist at Capital Economics.

“This supports our view that both real consumer spending and real GDP will grind to a halt in [the final quarter of this year and the first quarter of next]. And this fall in consumer confidence is also the kind of thing that makes the prime minister less likely to call an early election soon.”

Non-store retailing, predominantly online sales, fell 2.2% month on month, the biggest percentage fall across the retail sector.

Textile, clothing and footwear stores recorded a 0.9% fall, household goods retailers were hit by a 0.5% sales slump, while supermarkets dipped 0.4%, partly because of poor sales of clothing ranges due to the weather.

The only sector to record an increase in sales last month – apart from automotive fuel – was department stores, where the volume of goods bought rose 0.2%.

The fall in monthly sales follows a bumper August, with the ONS revising figures up from a 0.5% monthly rise to 0.7% .

This helped fuel a 0.7% increase in sales over the three months to the end of September compared with the previous quarter.

“Retail sales grew in the latest quarter with growth led by motor fuel, which, despite recent price increases at the pump, have now returned to monthly sales levels last seen before the start of the conflict in the Middle East,” said Hannah Finselbach, a senior statistician at the ONS. “Food and drink sales also contributed to growth in the quarter, partly helped by the warm weather and the World Cup, although they fell back slightly in September.”

title: Boom in weight-loss drugs could lead to fall in beer sales, Heineken warns UK pubs
author: Mark Sweney
text:
World’s second largest brewer says use of drugs such as Wegovy can reduce desire to drink alcohol

Heineken has warned British bars and pubs that the boom in popularity of weight-loss drugs could lead to a fall in sales of beer and cider.

The world’s second-largest brewer sent a presentation to British hospitality customers earlier this month that said the use of GLP-1 medication – such as Ozempic and Wegovy – could reduce the desire to drink alcohol . This in turn could result in “fullness and fewer serves” of pints in pubs and bars, it added.

The document, revealed by Reuters, said the GLP-1 era could lead to the tradition of the multi-pint drinking session becoming a less frequent occurrence.

The Netherlands-headquartered company offered advice including promoting half pints, low- and zero-alcohol options and pairing drinks with small plates of food, or risk declines in customer visits and spending.

“We see some changes in consumption behaviour among (GLP-1) users and will continue to monitor how these behaviours evolve in 2027,” said a Heineken spokesperson. “Consumer behaviour is evolving in response to a range of broader trends. GLP-1 is one of the developments we are monitoring.”

GLP-1 use has soared as consumers seek a quick solution to weight loss , with 10 million people turning to medication in the US last year, according to research by JP Morgan.

Heineken said the presentation was shared with customers as part of its regular engagement with UK businesses to help them understand how consumer habits were evolving.

Trends the brewer has identified in GLP-1 users include opting for smaller serves, lower alcohol drinks and more premium products.

“Our latest consumer research suggests GLP-1 users are not simply replacing alcohol,” said the spokesperson. “They are becoming more purposeful in their choices and broadening their preferences. These behaviours are not unique to GLP-1 users. They reflect broader consumer trends towards health and wellbeing, moderation, choice and more intentional consumption that we are seeing across our markets.”

As well as its eponymous lager, Heineken also owns brands such as Amstel, the Mexican lager Sol and Strongbow cider.

The Guinness maker, Diageo, has told investors that any impact from GLP-1 drugs becoming mainstream should be manageable, while Carlsberg told Reuters that data did not support the view that the use of weight-loss drugs affected beer consumption trends.

However, surveys by research companies including Circana, NIQ and KAM have pointed to reduced drinking by GLP-1 users.

According to Heineken, there was almost £14bn in sales of beer in British pubs, bars and restaurants in the year to February, with less than £300m of that from no- and low-alcohol products.

title: ‘Overnight, everything was dead’: the Teesside fisherman turned activist dubbed the Mr Bates of the seas
author: Robyn Vinter
text:
When thousands of dying crabs washed up on a Yorkshire beach in 2021, Stan Rennie’s livelihood was immediately threatened. Five years later, he’s leading the fight back against toxic ocean pollution – and corporate coverups

It was an otherwise typical day on 25 September 2021 when thousands of dead and dying crustaceans washed up on beaches in Yorkshire and the north-east of England. Early morning walkers and swimmers were aghast to find a sickening carpet of twitching, fitting crabs.

It would be the first but not the last die-off, which would see the disappearance of vast swathes of integral native sea life along an extended stretch of coast, including seal pups. It would also see the decimation of the local fishing industry and, with that, a way of life.

Environmentalists, fishers and ordinary local people wondered what could have possibly caused such a rare catastrophic incident. Meanwhile, hours before – completely coincidentally, the authorities said – a major dredging operation was carried out in the mouth of the River Tees, disturbing sediment where decades earlier highly toxic pollutants from heavy industry had been pumped.

The authorities, after carrying out a series of their own tests, denied there was a causal link, blaming an algae bloom and then, later, a novel pathogen. But those who live and work around the Tees estuary disagreed.

In All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea, the critically acclaimed documentary film-maker Jeanie Finlay is not setting out to find out what killed the crabs and lobsters. “I can’t offer an easy answer to what happened,” she says. “There isn’t an official cause. But what I can do is show the audience what that feels like.”

To do so, Finlay followed Stan Rennie, a fisher off the Teesside coast, over four years. What emerges is not an investigation into what destroyed precious marine life along a whole coastline but a story about the people searching for those answers. And it has won critics over. Mark Kermode called the film “a life-affirming treat – funny, poignant and profound”, and it was awarded early film festival gongs at Bristol and the Mediterrane.

Rennie is, according to Tina Brown, “the next Mr Bates”, and much like the Horizon Post Office scandal , it is a story of ordinary working people whose livelihoods have been destroyed, who are doggedly trying to get to the truth amid cold, uncaring powers that be.

In fact, it was the ITV series Mr Bates vs The Post Office that helped Finlay gain the trust of the group of jaded fishers, who by then had begun to believe nothing would change and resisted having their first meeting filmed. “After that came out, they were like, yeah you can film it,” says Finlay, who plays down her own role in endearing herself to the men, none of whom had seen – or, she says, had a particular interest in seeing – her 10 previous films.

They include Seahorse (2019) , following Freddy McConnell, a transgender man who gave birth, and, the same year, a documentary following the filming of the final series of Game of Thrones, lauded by critics as better than the season it documented.

But it was important too that Finlay is a local lass, having grown up in Stockton-on-Tees. When she first came across the story, it “made me think about the coastline that I knew and loved, the place that made me”. “I didn’t have to research it because I knew them. I knew them really, really well because this is my home,” she says.

We are introduced to Rennie in the opening scenes, as he explains from his boat, “All my life’s just been about fishing.” This is palpable over a video call from his home in Teesside, as he rattles off fishing jargon, in among complex scientific explanations and legal and bureaucratic terms in a whirlwind, telling the story of the past five years of his life.

He had pulled in some lobster pots that day in 2021 to find only dead lobsters in there. “We just knew that there was something wrong. Within a couple of days, the life had disappeared totally.”

It was disturbing, he says, to speak to his friends and realise they too had seen the devastation. “I got involved from then onwards, doing everything I could to campaign to get to the truth.”

Rennie has spent decades caring profoundly about the sealife on his doorstep. He would fish a mile away from the entrance of the Tees, in what had been some of the richest lobster grounds in the UK, thanks to sustainable fishing practices. “In all my life I’ve never kept a big lobster,” he says, explaining the process of cutting a v-shaped notch in the tails of large females and returning them to the sea. V-notched lobsters are illegal to sell in parts of the UK, so this act prevents them from ever being eaten, protecting them their entire 50-year lifespans.

“We could have landed thousands of lobsters, but we thought we were doing our bit and it certainly seemed to be working. And then overnight, all of them years, you think, what have we achieved? Because everything was dead.”

He is both the natural and reluctant leader of the North East Fishing Collective (NEFC), a group made up of about 60 fishers, many of whom found themselves swamped with debt and unable to take care of their families. Rennie is joined in his quest by Dr Sue Wilson from Tara Seal Research, who watched all the seal pups born along that same coastline perish, , chemist Dr Simon Gibbon and marine biologist Dr Gary Caldwell.

Another key figure, snippets of whom we see interspersed throughout, is the Tees Valley mayor Ben Houchen, now the Conservative Lord Houchen. He led the concerningly fast demolition of the old steelworks – featuring the largest UK explosion in 75 years – and rapid construction of the Teesside Freeport project in its place.…

title: Is a job guarantee the solution to mass AI unemployment?
author: Nick Romeo
text:
An old idea springs anew as a chorus of influential voices predicts that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitude

In a preface to his book Capitalism and Freedom, the American economist Milton Friedman famously observed that a crisis can propel once-fringe ideas into the political mainstream.

“Only a crisis – actual or perceived – produces real change. When that crisis occurs, the actions that are taken depend on the ideas that are lying around,” he wrote. The job of intellectuals, thinktanks and economists, he argued, is to refine the quality of these ambient ideas, so that good ones are ready when disaster strikes.

A chorus of influential voices is now predicting that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitude. Bill Gates has declared that AI will advance so rapidly that within a decade, humans will not be needed “for most things”. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has warned that the technology could cause widespread unemployment within one to five years, eliminating many positions in law, tech, finance and other white-collar professions. Even if these predictions are wrong, investors who bet heavily on the technology may conclude that AI is a bubble, and this in itself could cause a recession and widespread job loss.

Whether a crisis of mass AI-related job loss turns out to be actual or perceived, one policy idea that is attracting growing attention and support could directly mitigate this problem: a job guarantee.

In its most ambitious form, such a program would ensure that anyone who wants work is guaranteed a meaningful, decently paid job. By creating a public option for employment, its supporters argue, a job guarantee could protect millions of people from the financial and psychological damage of joblessness and mobilize a vast labor force to tackle urgent societal problems, from infrastructure and climate adaptation to elder care and childcare.

The concept of a job guarantee has a long history, both as an ideal and an actual policy. Article 23 of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights states: “Everyone has the right to work, to free choice of employment, to just and favourable conditions of work and to protection against unemployment.” During the Great Depression in the 1930s, Franklin D Roosevelt established the Works Progress Administration (WPA), which employed millions of Americans in ambitious public works projects that constructed roads, bridges, sewers, playing fields and much more. More recently, France , India and Argentina are among the countries that have launched versions of a job guarantee.

Though a job guarantee and universal basic income (UBI) are often grouped together, a recent global survey found greater support for job guarantees than UBIs. Polling of Americans by the Democratic strategist David Shor also shows the same pattern , with greater support for the creation of well-paid jobs than for direct income support. This makes sense, the venture capitalist and civic activist Nick Hanauer said, because “jobs represent so much more than income in human societies. They represent connection and dignity and enfranchisement and participation.”

Algernon Austin, director for race and economic justice at the Center for Economic and Policy Research, agreed: “A job guarantee is significantly preferable to UBI because work is more than just income. When you have a job, you gain work experience and you gain skills and you gain a network.”

Calculating the cost of a job guarantee depends on a holistic assessment of its impacts. During a US Senate hearing on affordability in June, John Kennedy, a Republican senator for Louisiana, suggested that a job guarantee would cost trillions of dollars and was impossible. When Dr Julie Margetta Morgan, president of the public policy thinktank the Century Foundation, told Kennedy that she supported a federal job guarantee, he replied : “Do you believe in the Easter bunny?”

Economists who study job guarantees see the calculation of costs and benefits differently. Max Kasy, a professor of economics at Oxford who has studied a recent job guarantee experiment in Austria, said that while the wages a job guarantee pays participants comprise a cost, such programs also save money in multiple ways.

“The cost saving comes from the fact that you don’t have to pay unemployment benefits, or maybe disability benefits or early retirement benefits. Then people who are working pay taxes and make social insurance contributions, so that’s additional revenue for the state. And then they hopefully do something that’s actually useful for society,” he said.

Participants in the job guarantee experiment in Austria also experienced social and psychological benefits . While the monetary value of greater wellbeing may be hard to quantify, such intangibles are crucial, according to Pavlina Tcherneva, a professor of economics at Bard College.

“Providing a good job to a person is absolutely transformative,” she said. Factoring in the costs of health problems that come from precarious unemployment and long-term unemployment, she added, makes the policy even more attractive, saying: “It’s not only affordable, it’s an investment.”

In September, the US representative Ayanna Pressley, a Democrat from Massachusetts, reintroduced a congressional resolution calling for the creation of a federal job guarantee, something she first proposed in 2021. Her proposal would create a federally funded but locally administered job guarantee that pays participants at least $25 an hour, with regular adjustments to reflect the rising cost of living. The jobs would include a range of sectors, such as emergency preparedness, relief and recovery after natural disasters, care for children and seniors, and public art projects modelled on the WPA’s popular Federal Art Project.…

title: "It's pretty bad" – Why Norris needs headache tablets for bumpy Austin circuit
America must reverse Trump’s moral squalor | Robert Reich
author: Robert Reich
text:
The president shows a unique disregard for the opinions, norms and ideals of the nation – and, for that matter, humanity

T he Democrats’ focus on affordability seems to be a winning strategy (we’ll know for sure in a little over two weeks). But we mustn’t lose sight of the moral squalor at the core of the Trump regime and the necessity of ending it.

It’s that moral squalor – the utter disregard for the opinions, norms and ideals of the nation and, for that matter, of humanity – that uniquely marks Trump and the reprobates he has attracted to Washington. It has also poisoned much of the Republican party, including the billionaires and tech bros who finance it.

To put this despicable era behind us, we’ll need to renounce and reverse this squalor.

What are loosely described as Trump’s “conflicts of interest”, for example, extend way beyond enriching himself from his presidency. He has violated the norms of presidential decency.

He recently decided to host the Group of 20 annual summit of world leaders at his private golf club in Miami in December. When he sought to do this during his first term, it was viewed as a blatant violation of the emoluments clause of the constitution. Now, after America’s moral sensibilities have been numbed by Trump’s appetite for foreign gifts – such as Qatar’s “donation” of a $400m jumbo jet – it barely merits a mention.

Trump’s social media platform Truth Social could reportedly charge up to $100,000 a month for access to “Truth API”, a service that gives subscribers access to potentially market-moving posts by high-profile users such as Trump “in milliseconds”. The service, in other words, enables subscribers to make lucrative stock market trades off market-moving information coming from the president.

A company linked to his family files a trademark application for “Trump TV” to control the name of a streaming service that the White House uses for official presidential communications, thereby pocketing the benefits from taxpayer funds used to create and run the channel.

His family-backed crypto firm introduces a stablecoin just months before he signs legislation promoting that type of cryptocurrency . His wife is paid tens of millions for a self-promotional film by Jeff Bezos’s Amazon, a federal contractor and major retailer subject to a myriad of regulations. His son has a Russian oligarch , close to Putin, pick up the tab for part of his wedding afterparty in the Bahamas.

He arranges for the justice department to grant him and his family immunity for any back taxes and penalties they might owe.

And so on. Trump has tossed away all constraints on making money off his presidency “because I got no credit in the first term” and “I found out that nobody cared”.

Credit? Someone who is entrusted with the highest office in the land must receive “credit” for doing what’s right, in order to continue doing what’s right? Nobody cares? A president can embrace corruption if the public doesn’t mind?

It’s not just the blatant self-dealing. His moral squalor extends to every aspect of governing.

He lies incessantly – a gushing firehose of deception.

His foreign policies make Henry Kissinger’s realpolitik seem principled by comparison. He orders the abduction of the president of another nation, installs a new president of his choosing, and announces he’s taking that nation’s oil – and doesn’t even account for what he does with the oil money.

He attacks Iran without consulting America’s traditional allies or even Congress.

He turns his back on Ukraine and sides with Putin, the aggressor in that conflict. He pursues diesel oil from Putin in violation of US sanctions on Russia and blames the Ukrainian president , Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for high oil prices rather than Trump’s war on Iran. He says Ukraine should get a new president.

The moral squalor extends to usurping the authority of Congress to decide on tariffs, wars and whether and how to spend taxpayer money.

It extends to his cynical defiance of supreme court orders. When the court invalidates his tariffs, he reimposes them under a different statute. When the court rules that he doesn’t have grounds to remove a member of the Fed board of governors, he concocts a means to do so anyway. When the court says he has to remove his name from the Kennedy Center, he closes the center and threatens to demolish it .

It extends to his using the justice department and the FBI to prosecute people who have stood up to him, including courageous officials.

It extends to his claims that Mexicans are “bringing drugs and crime”; calling Somali-Americans “ garbage ” and denouncing “what they’ve done to Minnesota, these people from Somalia”; and taunting Muslims, including by calling Dr Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate from Michigan, “ Mohammed ”.

It extends to giving a gigantic tax cut to America’s wealthiest people, financed by cutting nutrition assistance and healthcare to America’s most vulnerable people.

The moral squalor has turned much of America into a police state – terrorizing large numbers of people residing here, including many here legally.

Deploying ICE agents at schools, courthouses and hospitals. Forcibly taking parents away from their children. Allowing masked gunmen without identification to grab suspected undocumented immigrants off our streets, from their cars, and out of their homes – giving them no opportunity to defend themselves in front of third parties before putting them into often overcrowded and unhealthy prisons or sending them to other countries where they’re imprisoned. Killing people.

When asked if there are limits to his authority, Trump replies : “Yeah, there is one thing. My own morality. My own mind. It’s the only thing that can stop me.”…

title: The Knicks finally got their rings, the coaches got boxes
author: Russell Richardson
text:
Empty ring boxes and fake offers. Even a title couldn’t cure everything that’s wrong at MSG.

Imagine your employer had an excellent year and you were in line for an award, one you earned through great effort, extensive travel, and long nights. Instead of receiving it, however, you’re handed an IOU note at the ceremony. Or worse, you were gotcha-ed with a fake email about the award, just to test the company’s cybersecurity.

Your response might justifiably range “from genuine anger to annoyance,” as Joe Vardon of The Athletic puts it .

When Vardon describes this very scenario in his latest report, he’s not talking about the slighted workers of a local plumbing supply company. He’s talking about the assistant coaches and staff of the world champion New York Knicks.

At Tuesday’s season opener, the presentation (broadcast nationally on NBC) made it appear the Knicks assistant coaches were receiving championship rings during the pregame banner ceremony. The boxes they were handed? Empty.

It came as no surprise to the assistants. They hadn’t even been fitted for rings, and the empty boxes were a token gesture so they wouldn’t feel left out. Token gestures can backfire on you, though, especially when they seem, perhaps, insincere. The Knicks coaches were upset, according to Vardon, on a scale from mild irritation to very spicy.

In quintessential Knicks fashion, the organization’s statement on the situation is, “We are not disclosing anything about the rings.” Because robots need not acknowledge the petty concerns of disposable humans.

One of the most stunning quotes from Vardon’s piece is this:

“ The Athletic received conflicting information about whether head coach Mike Brown received his ring on Tuesday and could not immediately verify if he got one.”

What? We can’t confirm if coach Mike Brown got a ring? What??

The story careens off a cliff from there. Vardon notes, “Many longtime employees at Madison Square Garden, including some who work in the Knicks’ business operations, will not receive rings at all […]. Typically, most employees for NBA teams receive rings, even if they are not as fancy and expensive as the ones the players receive.” Yes, some franchises reward the plebes, but not the NBA’s second-most valuable one. Enter Gordon Gekko, stage left.

However, in September, MSG sent employees a fake championship ring offer. The email congratulated recipients and invited them to select one of two complimentary ring designs: “Championship Gold” or “Garden Classic.” But ha on you, fools! The email was actually an internal phishing test. Employees who clicked the link were assigned mandatory cybersecurity training rather than receive a ring.

What kind of cold, villainous monster says, “You know how we’re not giving the employees championship rings? One hilarious way to test our cybersecurity would be….”

Oh, the team ain’t hurting for money. The Knicks reportedly generated $640 million in revenue during their championship season, while the franchise’s estimated valuation climbed 29% to $12.6 billion, making it the NBA’s second-most valuable team.

Giving New York the benefit of the doubt, those rings must be difficult to manufacture. Designed by Jason Arasheben of Jason of Beverly Hills, the Knicks’ blingy ring features roughly 800 diamonds and sapphires totaling 22 carats, set in white gold. Its elaborate design includes a mechanical pop-up replica of Madison Square Garden, 16 emerald-cut diamonds representing the team’s playoff victories, and a 0.16-carat diamond set in the Larry O’Brien Trophy. One cannot gaze for long upon the ring before weeping, and it must be returned to Mount Doom post haste!

The Knicks won in mid-June, leaving about four months for design, contract, and construction. That’s a tight schedule. Delays aren’t unprecedented in the NBA, and according to team sources, the assistants will eventually receive rings. Still, other championship teams have distributed coaches’ rings on opening night, so…

Who are we talking about, exactly? The championship coaching staff included associate head coach Chris Jent, assistants Rick Brunson, Mark Bryant, Darren Erman, Riccardo Fois, Brendan O’Connor, and TJ Saint, along with several player development coaches and advisors (including one of the greatest names in NBA history, the legendary Mo Cheeks!). These were among the people who helped deliver New York’s first NBA championship in 53 years.

To recap: What should have been a celebration of the Knicks’ victory instead exposed tiresome and familiar organizational dysfunction, with coaches handed empty boxes and longtime employees subjected to a misleading phishing exercise. Team owner James Dolan proves once again to be tone-deaf, and this time not by singing at the mic.

A franchise worth billions, a championship decades in the making, and apparently not enough goodwill to go around. How come they win it all and still feel like LOLKnicks?

Read Vardon’s full article here . Go Knicks.

title: Anti-Pogačar? Not quite, but this radical Tour de France route does highlight ASO's love-hate relationship with the world's best rider
author: Patrick Fletcher
text:
You might have seen the 2027 Tour de France route described as an 'anti-Pogačar' exercise, and, with a return to time trialling doses of old and a relatively meagre helping of high mountains, you can certainly see why.

In truth, there is no such thing as an 'anti-Pogačar' route. It simply does not exist within the realms of plausible conception. It would have to be 21 flat stages, half of them against the clock, and even then he’d still probably find a way to win.

And yet, the route that was unveiled in Paris on Thursday did signal a growing discomfort, on the part of the Tour de France organisers, with Tadej Pogačar ’s dominance. Jonas Vingegaard’s epic takedowns of the Slovenian are three years in the past now, and Pogačar has since rattled off a trio of yellow jerseys, each more convincing than the last, to take his tally to a record-equalling five.

He has done so with the sort of panache the race directors can only dream of, but he has also done it with a level of ease that is becoming a bit of a nightmare. So utterly superior, Pogačar spent the second half of this year’s Tour essentially riding as a domestique for his third-placed teammate, Isaac del Toro. In some ways, the yellow jersey selflessly repaying favours is a nice image for the race. In others ways, it’s really not such a great look – not one you’d want to make a habit of, anyway.

The irony was that the 2026 Tour de France had been billed as a 'Tour of Suspense'. The route had been constructed in such a way, we were told, that the battle for yellow would only be decided in the final days on Alpe d’Huez. As it turned out, Pogačar had the jersey all but sewn up by stage 6.

I wrote a piece on this at the time – about how the attempt to tone down the early Col du Tourmalet only toned it up – so I won’t rehash it all here, but it was a bit of an own goal, I felt. Granted, Pogačar’s dominance would have told anyway, but in any case, it was revealing in the broader context of ASO’s intentions.

Put simply, they badly want a yellow jersey contest that remains open until the last few days, and it didn’t work last time.

Not a good year to be a polka-dot fan

And so here we are, not going above 1,750 metres of altitude until stage 18 of 21 next July.

The route for that stage is a Pyrenean beast – going over the Soulor, Tourmlaet, and Hourquette d’Ancizan before the final climb to the Col du Portet – but it makes everything else look pretty tame in comparison. In fact, it’s only the second of two true mountain-top finishes in the entire race.

The Alps have had it pretty good in recent years but what did they do to deserve this? Even if the World Champs-inspired stage 10 looks like a thriller and the stage 11 combo of the Col du Pré and Montée de Bisanne looks tough enough, the lack of big-name high-altitude Alpine passes is really quite shocking.

And the Pyrenees may have the upper hand this time but they too only have two stages. Elsewhere, it’s over to the Jura to provide the first summit finish on the Grand Colombier on stage 9, and the Massif Central on a stage 14 that is harder than it looks but still very much sloggy medium mountain stuff. All in all, then, not a good year to be a die-hard polka-dot fan.

And then there’s the time trialling, with 71km against the clock constituting the most ITT-heavy Tour de France since the former world TT champion Bradley Wiggins won the race in 2012. This itself is remarkable, a complete laying down of arms in the battle ASO has waged on time trialling over the past decade. This was, of course, inspired by the dominance of Team Sky – first through Wiggins and then through Chris Froome and Geraint Thomas – but the trend has remained even in the Pogačar and Vingegaard era.

Until now. It’s no coincidence that the runner-up this year is also the best time triallist in the world, by a country mile. Remco Evenepoel may well wear the yellow jersey in next year’s Tour, and he may well take a minute or two on Pogačar, though it’s worth remembering he was beaten by more than six this summer (with Pogačar taking his foot off the gas at times).

So you can’t Pogačar-proof a Tour de France route, but in completely upending the balance between mountains and time trials, the organisers have certainly taken a new, much bolder, step in attempting to prevent him completely running away with it.

Pro-Pogačar, anti-Vingegaard?

At this point, it’s worth circling back to ASO’s relationship with Pogačar, which we might describe as 'love-hate'. They hate the suspense he takes away from the race as a whole, but they absolutely love just about everything else about him.

Race director Christian Prudhomme and co barely made any attempt to hide their distaste of the so-called Skybots, and what an antidote they’ve since struck upon with Pogačar, an all-action figure who will light up the race given even the slightest invitation, or even the slightest hint of boredom. For two years in a row now he has been in the thick of the action on the remodelled final stage over the Montmartre climb in Paris, carrying the Classics torch that has seen him win Milan-San Remo, the Tour of Flanders, and twice podium Paris-Roubaix.

In that respect, this is actually quite a pro-Pogačar route. The entire first week is peppered with punchy climbs and Classics-flavoured stages that aren’t critical GC flashpoints but may well tempt Pogačar out to play. The first of the two Alpine stages, based on the route for World Championships past and future, looks like the sort of circuit-based, short-but-hard-climb affair Pogačar would draw up in his dreams.

The marquee high-mountain stages have been toned down only because the terrain dictates that this is where his superiority stretches into big time differences. But for all Pogačar is the best climber in the world, he’s not a pure climber, and he has famously come unstuck on some of the Tour’s most brutal mountain stages. Vingegaard was the man to crack him in both 2022 and 2023, and while the Dane hasn’t come close in recent years, he has mitigating circumstances, not least the fact that he didn’t get to finish this year’s race.

For many years now, Vingegaard has banged out the same old refrain – that he can only try and live with Pogačar on the punchier climbing days, and that he needs the bigger, heavier, multi-col mountain days to truly take the fight to him.

In that light, the 2027 Tour de France route only reduces the room for manouevre for the greatest rival of Pogačar’s career. Of course, with Paul Seixas coming through, that title could change hands at some point, and it’s worth noting that the French prodigy – already a winner at Il Lombardia and runner-up at Liège and Strade Bianche – is cut from very much the same cloth as Pogačar.

But no, if this route is anti-anyone, it’s anti-Vingegaard. And if you were the Dane, seeing your favored terrain neglected as Evenepoel’s is pandered to – by people who want a closer challenge to Pogačar – you might just take that personally.

As for main man himself, we return to the point we made at the start of this piece; you could devise 100 different Tour de France routes, and the Tadej Pogačar of the past three years would win every single time, provided he stays upright.

And here again Prudhomme made a revealing comment. " There are certainly questions lingering after his crash ," the race director said of Pogačar’s season-ending Vuelta fall, even going as far as to reference Eddy Merckx’s famous (and much more severe) 1969 crash, after which he was supposedly never the same rider (but still won four more Tours). Prudhomme seems excited by that prospect of a slightly-less-than-perfect Pogačar, or at least relishing the doubt, the intrigue, the… suspense.

Whether we actually get any of the stuff next July remains to be seen. The Tour de France organisers love Tadej Pogačar, but they hate him too, and it seems even clearer now that they want the best of best worlds – to encourage his firework-lighting instincts while at the same time trying to rein him in to some degree.

In that respect, the 2027 Tour de France route is one of the most radical we’ve seen in years – it simply might not make a blind bit of difference.

title: Should Man Utd boss Carrick drop captain Fernandes?
text:
Michael Carrick is never short of advice around how he should do his job as head coach of Manchester United.

Few of his players divide opinion quite so much as skipper Bruno Fernandes.

So, it stands to reason there are a variety of views around whether Fernandes should be dropped for Sunday's vital Premier League game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

Former Everton and Rangers striker Duncan Ferguson has no doubts.

"It is a big problem for Michael," he told The Overlap podcast. "Put people in the team you trust. Your captain has thrown you under the bus. If you don't think he is playing for you, get him out. I wouldn't pick him even though he is their best player."

Joe Smith, respected host of Manchester United fan channel Stretford Paddock, is of the same opinion.

"I don't think Fernandes should play on the weekend," he said. "I don't think (Lisandro) Martínez should've played against Leeds, because otherwise they're running the ship here."

United fans heading back on flights from Como to Manchester had a view, although much of it was wrapped up in their general thoughts about the club, most of which were negative.

But only one man's opinion really counts. Carrick is the man who picks the team.

His friend and former team-mate Wayne Rooney has a view on that.

"When Martinez came out, I said this is an absolute nightmare because it will rip the dressing room apart," he said on the United Stand podcast.

"That was the start. We've seen it now with Bruno and you're going to see it with more players because they don't want to take responsibility.

"I was in that situation [as manager at Plymouth and Birmingham City] and if I was in Carrick's position now, I'd come out fighting. There's no more Mr Nice Guy."

Carrick is due to speak in a news conference to preview the Bournemouth game at 1330 BST.

He will be asked whether Bruno Fernandes is going to be dropped.

Many observers were shocked to discover Fernandes was not going to be disciplined for his post-match outburst following the 4-1 Champions League defeat by Como. They were also surprised that he would remain as Manchester United skipper, when team-mate Lisandro Martinez was fined for attacking the club hierarchy eight days earlier after the 2-0 loss to Atletico Madrid.

"It was an assassination," one source who has worked with Fernandes previously, told BBC Sport of Wednesday's comments.

"It was unprofessional. Michael's team are killing him."

The issue is whether Fernandes went too far in attacking Carrick's tactics for the Como game, then saying it was on the coaching team on the sidelines to spot the problem and change it, not the players.

Fernandes is one of the most knowledgeable members of Carrick's squad when it comes to football tactics, and is desperate to succeed. His comments, made on TNT Sports weren't off the cuff, or said in an emotional state after a defeat, as Lisandro Martinez's were.

Yet there is also sympathy for Fernandes from some at Old Trafford given the 32-year-old carried out 10 post-match interviews after the Como debacle, and also because, while hardly offering a defence of Carrick, the words were less inflammatory when they were spoken as they seem in text form.

It is easy to point to Sir Alex Ferguson, the former Manchester United manager who was a strong advocate of managers needing to have control over their players and wonder how he would have reacted to such a situation. Challenges to his authority tended to end with players leaving the club.

However, you only need to listen to Gordon Strachan recounting instances from Ferguson's time in charge at Aberdeen on 'The Good, The Bad and the Football podcast' to accept some of the Scot's more extreme methods would not be acceptable in the current climate.

United's hierarchy are keen to get away from the cycle of sacking managers, having dismissed Ruben Amorim last season and Erik ten Hag in the one before.

However, there is also a basic truth that Carrick desperately needs to end the present run of seven games without a win. If they fail against Bournemouth it would equal the sorry run of Louis van Gaal in 2015-16, which was the worst since a Ferguson-led side had eight draws and a defeat during the 1988-89 season.

So, with Benjamin Sesko, Kobbie Mainoo and Marcus Rashford all ruled out through injury, can Carrick drop Fernandes even if he wanted to?

The Portuguese's link-up with Youri Tielemans has not flourished as imagined.

And the only goal contributions by last season's PFA player of the year have been a hat-trick and assist in the 5-2 win over Ipswich in August and his strike against Azerbaijan champions Sabah FK on 10 September.

But, as Duncan Ferguson said, he is their best player. Carrick has to make the call. He needs to get it right.
