title: Eddie Howe is Jason Wilcox’s choice if Manchester United replace Michael Carrick
author: Jamie Jackson
text:
Howe would seriously consider job if offered it

Head of recruitment Vivell prefers Julian Nagelsmann

Eddie Howe is the current preferred candidate of Jason Wilcox to replace Michael Carrick should Manchester United decide to change manager, with the director of football believing Howe’s extensive Premier League experience places him ahead of other potential targets.

Howe left Newcastle in late July to take a break from the game but would seriously consider a return for the United role, it is understood, should this be offered.

Howe would be less expensive to bring in than Unai Emery, another admired candidate, because Aston Villa would demand about £20m in compensation for their manager.

In five years managing Newcastle Howe impressed, leading the team to the 2025 Carabao Cup, ending a 70-year wait for a domestic trophy. After taking over from Steve Bruce in November 2021, Howe led Newcastle to 11th, winning 12 of the last 18 games. The team had gone 14 games without a victory at the start of the season.

Howe also took Newcastle back into the Champions League after 20 years in 2023 and qualified again two seasons later. He managed Bournemouth for five seasons in the Premier League from 2015.

Julian Nagelsmann, the former Germany and Bayern Munich coach, is highly regarded by Christopher Vivell, United’s head of recruitment, but Wilcox’s view may hold more sway with Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who controls football policy.

Carrick is under serious pressure after the club’s poorest start since 1986. The 45-year-old is expected to remain in place for Sunday’s visit of Bournemouth – he is due to hold his pre-game media conference on Friday – but the 45-year-old’s job is in the balance after two wins from 11 games this season.

United are inviting fans to offer their views on the design of the proposed new 100,000-seat stadium. A survey will be sent to season-ticket holders, cup season-ticket holders, executive club members, official members, supporters who have purchased hospitality at Old Trafford within the past three years and season-ticket waiting list members.

title: What is the Budget and what could be in it?
text:
Chancellor John Healey will set out Labour's tax and spending plans when he delivers his first Budget on 28 October.

He has refused to rule out tax increases after acknowledging government borrowing costs are at "historic highs".

But the government's room for manoeuvre on tax is limited.

Before the 2024 general election, Labour promised not to increase three big revenue earners for the government: income tax, National Insurance and VAT.

In his statement, delivered to MPs in the House of Commons, Healey will set out how the government plans to raise or lower taxes.

Alongside the Budget, the Treasury will publish details about the measures and their costs.

The independent Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), which monitors government spending, will also publish an assessment of the health of the UK economy and a forecast of what it thinks will happen in the future.

The run-up to the Budget typically generates speculation about what might be in it, which the government is trying to keep to a minimum this year.

Healey and Prime Minister Andy Burnham face a difficult balancing act, trying to offer more support to households and meet commitments on defence spending, while also sticking to Labour's manifesto commitments on tax and the government's self-imposed fiscal rules.

The previous chancellor, Rachel Reeves, set out two main rules, which the new leadership has vowed to follow. These are:

Not to borrow to fund day-to-day public spending by the end of this parliament

To get government debt falling as a share of national income by the end of this parliament

In March, the OBR calculated that the first rule would be met with a gap - or headroom - of £23.6bn. However, this headroom is expected to have shrunk.

Analysts are divided on how much it may have fallen by. KPMG believe it could have fallen to £12bn, mainly due to the rise in government borrowing costs this year.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) also forecasts that debt interest will significantly reduce headroom. But it also suggests higher inflation could push up tax revenues as pay rises drag people into higher tax thresholds.

It estimates the buffer could still shrink but to a comparatively less severe £20bn.

One option that has been floated is that Healey could decide to accept a smaller buffer, reducing the need to increase taxes in the Budget.

Bank bosses have told the BBC they expect Healey to raise taxes on the sector . UK banks have been reporting bumper profits, leading to calls from unions for higher taxes.

The Treasury has options: it could raise a 3% surcharge on profits which was lowered from 8% under the previous Conservative government, or it could raise the bank levy that is based on the size of their balance sheets.

Further details on the "Your First Home" scheme, aimed at helping first-time buyers in England to purchase a property, are expected to be announced in the Budget.

The scheme will allow people to buy a new-build home with a deposit of 2.5%. It would provide them with a loan worth 20% of their property's value to help pay for the purchase.

There has been speculation that Capital Gains Tax (CGT) - which is imposed on the profit people make when they sell an asset that has increased in value - could be changed, through either higher rates or by removing or amending exemptions.

At the moment, if you pay income tax at the basic rate then CGT is charged at 18%. For higher and additional rate income tax payers, the CGT rate is 24%.

The FT has reported , external that Healey has rejected proposals to raise CGT to the same rates as income tax.

The Times has reported , external that online retail giants such as Amazon and eBay are expected to be made responsible for collecting tax owed by traders using their platforms.

The paper said the money raised is expected to be used by the government to cut business rates for High Street shops, by raising the threshold at which small companies start paying rates from £12,000 to £18,000.

Fuel duty was frozen under the Conservatives in March 2022 and Sir Keir Starmer's government continued the freeze, deciding in May to push back a planned 3p increase in September until the end of this year.

Healey told the BBC in late September that the "place" and "time" for dealing with rising petrol and diesel costs was the Budget, but would not give details on whether the freeze would be extended again.

Household energy bills are set to see their biggest rise in four years in January, with a typical annual bill forecast to jump by £276 .

There has been speculation , external that Healey is planning energy bill help for households on certain benefits.

The High Value Council Tax Surcharge - dubbed the Mansion Tax - was announced in last year's Budget and will apply to properties in England valued above £2m from April 2028.

There had been speculation that the government was considering extending it to properties worth more than £1.5m. However, reports now suggest , external Healey has ruled this out.

In the first three months of the year, the UK's economy grew by 0.6%, while in the April-to-June quarter it grew by 0.5%.

The most recent data showed the economy grew by 0.1% in August after growth of 0.4% in July, with both figures being stronger than expected.

Analysts say the UK economy is proving resilient in the face of energy price shocks caused by the US-Israel war with Iran.

The conflict has led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for oil and gas trade. This caused a sharp jump in oil prices, which has fed through to higher energy and fuel prices.

Economists expect UK growth to slow in the months ahead as those costs continue to weigh on households and businesses.

Prices for goods and services are still rising faster than wanted. Inflation hit 3.1% in the year to August, the highest rate in five months and above the Bank of England's 2% target, driven by higher petrol and diesel prices.…

title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI
text:
Mohammed Ashim has been cutting hair and trimming beards for four years in Bengaluru.

But recently the 22-year old has been strapping a camera to his head to record his work.

The camera only records his hands and fingers - his client's faces are blurred out.

"The routine is simple, but you have to be disciplined about how you move. The operations team taught me that my hands always have to stay cleanly inside the frame, the lighting has to be sharp, and I can't tilt my head too abruptly while working."

He wears the camera for five or six hours a day.

"It's good money, but honestly, the feeling of doing something this futuristic is what keeps me excited. I never imagined my razor techniques would be useful to a global tech company," says Ashim.

He is one of hundreds of thousands of workers across the world paid to record their activities.

Ashim's footage is collected by a local company, which might have hundreds of people filming their work.

That video is then sold on to technology companies and research organisations who use it to train artificial intelligence - in particular so-called physical AI, a type of artificial intelligence that can control robots in the real world.

Rashdan Technologies collects and processes such human generated data.

"Every robotics company, every frontier AI lab, has a specific kind of data they want: industrial tasks, agriculture, household chores, small business work like pottery, garment-making, embroidery, candle-making. We go wherever the task is," says co-founder and CEO Shahil Baig.

His company pays $5 to $10 (£3.74; £7.47) for eight to 10 hours of recorded work.

"For a lot of these people, that's meaningful," Baig says.

Making sure workers give their consent and are comfortable with the process is important, he says.

"We record hands, not faces, and where multi-camera rigs do capture more of the body or environment, we blur faces out. No names, no contact details, nothing that identifies them personally goes into what we hand off."

But his customers are getting more demanding.

"Now clients are asking for four to six cameras rigged around a person's head to cover the entire scene, not just the hands.

"Getting someone to agree to one small camera is one conversation. Getting them to agree to wearing what's effectively a five-camera headset is a completely different, and harder, one. We pay more for that tier of data collection because of what we're asking of people."

And the industry is becoming more crowded, Agarwal expects dozens more competitors to emerge in India this year.

If you want robots to navigate the real world, they can't just be trained inside computer simulations, argues Manish Agarwal, the founder of Humyn Labs, which collects and processes human-generated data.

Most of that data comes from video, but sometimes collectors wear hardware on their hands and fingers to capture physical contact.

"Physical tasks require high-quality signals involving limb movements, fingers, wrists, elbows, shoulders and dynamic force application. For example: applying the correct grip force so a plastic bottle doesn't crumble versus a steel glass," he says.

And until recently, that data was not available.

"There is no existing internet archive of embodied human activity - no dataset of a kitchen being cleaned, or a car being assembled by hands that know exactly how much force to apply. That data has to be captured from scratch, in the real world, across diverse environments," says Agarwal, whose company has bases in Bangalore and San Francisco.

At the moment his firm has 96,000 data collectors across countries in Latin America and Southeast Asia.

Humyn Labs filters the thousands of hours of video supplied by those collectors, selecting the most useful content. It's then labelled so the AI knows what it is looking at and packaged in a format that can be used by clients.

"You need to source across a variety of factories, a variety of tasks, in different geographies because if you want to build deployment for US factories or US houses, you'd want environments that are a proxy for that. Residential houses in India may not be the right context for building a robotics use case for the US."

But are workers collecting data for machines that will one day do their jobs?

At the moment it's too early to tell says Bino Paul, senior professor at the School of Management and Labour Studies at the Tata Institute of Social Sciences (TISS) in Mumbai.

For some workers AI might be a useful tool, but robots could automate other jobs, he says.

The problem is that, if machines do start to take over, there will be little workers can do about.

"By the time workers realise what they have participated in, things may have gone too far," he says.

Like many others, he wants governments to regulate AI.

"AI cannot be viewed merely as a technical system. We need to develop a socio-technical system in which ethics is upheld through human agency, ensuring that AI delivers beneficence rather than maleficence."

Despite concerns over where AI is heading, money is still being poured into its development.

Some of that trickles down to workers in India, where there is no shortage of workers prepared to wear a camera for a few dollars a day.

Mohammed Arman has been working in the textiles industry in Bangalore for 10 years.

"Garments stitching and cutting. I know this work so well I could probably do it with my eyes closed. Cloth, thread, needle, machine after 10 years, your hands just know what to do before your mind even tells them," he says.

He has recently started wearing a head-mounted camera that records his work.

"For me, it's simple. This is survival. I have a family back home in Bihar, and every rupee I send back matters. If someone offers me extra money to wear a camera while I do the exact same work I've been doing for 10 years, I'm not going to say no.…

title: Magnitude-7 earthquake hits Tibet, killing at least 16 and destroying hundreds of homes
author: Associated Press
text:
Search and rescue efforts under way after quake strikes region’s north, officials say, while at least seven aftershocks recorded

A magnitude-7 earthquake has hit China’s Tibet region, killing at least 16 people, injuring 54 and collapsing hundreds of homes in the northern regional city of Nagqu, official media said.

Search and rescue efforts continued after the collapse of at least 339 homes and 20 livestock sheds, the Nagqu media office said, citing city government officials.

More than 1,600 people from the local county were deployed for rescue efforts. Supplies including 1,000 prefabricated housing units and about 3,000 tents and folding beds as well as torches and winter clothing arrived in the region.

The US Geological Survey said the quake occurred at 10.33pm local time on Thursday, with its epicentre 191km (119 miles) east-northeast of Nagqu, in a sparsely populated, high-altitude area of northern Tibet . It put the earthquake’s depth at 18km.

The US agency recorded at least seven aftershocks with magnitude between 4.3 and 5.2, all of them with a depth of 10km, according to its website.

Videos posted by China’s national broadcaster CCTV said showed workers running out of restaurants and objects falling off shelves at supermarkets when the quake struck.

China’s official Xinhua news agency said on Friday that communication in some areas hit by the quake was down. Local railway authorities had taken emergency actions to halt trains passing through the region.

More than 300 police officers had been dispatched for relief work while the regional fire and rescue corps has mobilised almost 350 personnel to the affected areas, Xinhua reported.

Rescue workers clambered through damaged buildings, some with collapsed roofs, footage on CCTV showed.

The earthquake also caused rockfalls that had forced local authorities to close a section of national highway 317, allowing only emergency, rescue and official support vehicles through as crews worked to clear debris, according to Xinhua.

Intermittent snows were expected in the quake region over the next three days, Xinhua said. It was the biggest quake in the region in the past five years, CCTV said.

China’s leader, Xi Jinping, called for all-out efforts in rescue operations and medical relief work.

Nagqu is more than 300km north of Tibet’s capital, Lhasa.

Earthquakes are relatively common in China. In January 2025, at least 126 people were killed in one in Tibet’s rural Tingri county.

In December 2023, a quake in remote Gansu province in north-west China killed at least 134 people, state media said. That quake was China’s deadliest since 2014, when more than 600 people died in the south-western province of Yunnan.

A huge tremor in Sichuan province in 2008 left approximately 90,000 people dead or missing, including about 5,000 schoolchildren.

title: 'I'm certainly not opposed to it' – Tim Merlier gives cautious thumbs up to teammate Paul Magnier joining him at 2027 Tour de France
author: Alasdair Fotheringham
text:
Triple 2026 Tour de France stage winner Tim Merlier (Soudal-QuickStep) has given a cautious welcome to the idea that up-and-coming French sprinter and teammate Paul Magnier might join him in the 2027 race.

Next July, it might be that the two race together in a Grand Tour for the first time.

At the Tour presentation this Thursday , Merlier himself played down the number of sprint stages on offer in the 2027 route but he did not roundly reject the idea of sharing those opportunities with Merlier.

"I have already discussed that with the team," Merlier said in comments reported by . "I am certainly not opposed to it. I think it would be possible.

"He is still young and I have the feeling that he still looks up to me; he sometimes still asks for tips. He could learn a lot from it."

Although the Belgian star argued that it was not necessarily a given that it would happen, concluding on that subject – and without explaining why – that “the chance that it actually happens seems quite small to me".

The other big subject on the virtual table for Merlier in Paris was whether he could take the yellow jersey in Carlisle at the end of day 1 of the 2027 Tour . Opportunities for sprinters to take the opening stage's yellow jersey are never high in the Tour and the sprint finish in Carlisle is a gradual uphill, exactly the kind that Merlier likes.

Furthermore, after missing out in Lille in 2025, the previous chance the fast men had to go for yellow in the Tour, Merlier recognised that he was looking forward to a fresh chance coming his way.

“It would be wonderful. I let it slip in Lille in 2025, so I’m happy to get a second chance already. Normally, that doesn’t happen very often," he said.

"It's a nice challenge for the sprinters, and it's not impossible it could happen."

It might sound surprising that Merlier was pleased that there were two time trials in the 2027 route, but that was more for practical reasons because he was suddenly going to switch specialities at 33. At the same time, he agreed with Mark Cavendish that if the sprinters' teams worked well enough, the last day over the Butte Montmartre in Paris could still end up being decided by a mass dash to the line on the Champs Élysées.

"Two time trials are two rest days for me," he reasoned, "and though I'd like to see a 'real' sprint without the Montmartre on the last day, if the sprinters' teams all work well together, it might still be possible that it happens."

It is true, too, that stage 21 breakaway winner Mathieu van der Poel (Alpecin-Premier Tech) only took the last dash for the line in Paris by the bare minimum ahead of teammate Jasper Philipsen last July. But in any case, rather than the seven sprints predicted by the Tour de France organisation on Thursday for 2027, Merlier says that he thinks a much smaller number is likely.

"If we can sprint four times, that would already be great. It all looks very tough. When you see the elevation gain [53,450 metres - Ed.] across the race, you don't get very excited as a sprinter," he said with a laugh.

title: India slashes cost of cancer drugs after court rules mark-ups are ‘extortion’
author: Amrit Dhillon in Delhi
text:
Case filed in 2022 by patient unable to afford medicine leads to cap on drug prices for millions who face ruin if diagnosed

The Indian government has moved to reduce the price of cancer drugs after a retired bank clerk took her case to the supreme court.

From next month, 137 cancer drugs in India will be cheaper as the government tries to tackle the tragedy of poorer patients either forgoing treatment, selling land or falling into debt to meet the high cost of some medicines, which are making large profits for hospitals and pharmacists.

Sarojam Radhakrishnan, a former bank employee in Kerala, was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2021. Doctors prescribed life-saving targeted treatments but the monthly cost, of more than 63,000 rupees (£500), was far beyond her family’s means.

Realising that thousands of families were being ruined by the cost of such drugs, Radhakrishnan filed a petition to the Kerala high court in 2022 demanding government intervention to lower the costs.

When the case reached the supreme court, the judges looked at hospitals’ and retailers’ mark-ups on cancer drugs and called the situation “carnage” and “extortion”.

During a hearing on 29 September, justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta noted how a life-saving cancer drug supplied to hospitals at 2,700 rupees carried a vastly marked-up price of 27,000 rupees .

The judges found that hospitals, distributors and chemists enjoyed large margins on medicines. Analysis by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority revealed a trade mark-up on some cancer drugs averaging 170% , with some extreme examples stretching to more than 700%.

A 30% trade margin cap on the price of 42 drugs has been in place for some years but many others remained off this list. Now, prodded by the supreme court’s findings, the government has imposed the cap on 137 other drugs.

“The measure is expected to reduce medicine prices by up to 70% and help cancer patients save 2,500 crore rupees [£199m] annually, significantly reducing the amount they pay from their own pockets,” a statement from the Department of Pharmaceuticals said.

People on low incomes in India dread illness, as the cost of treatment can mean financial ruin, particularly for cancer patients.

Whenever the Indian Cancer Society holds a free diagnosis camp in Gurgaon where he lives, Krishan Kalra urges local drivers, maids, cooks and tailors to turn up because tests they cannot afford are offered free.

As a former member of the council of the Rajiv Gandhi Cancer Institute and Research Centre, Kalra knows the importance of early diagnosis, but he said very few people attended. “When I ask why, they say they’re too scared – if something serious like cancer is detected, they haven’t got the money to pay for the treatment so they prefer to remain in the dark,” he said.

With the cost of cancer drugs ranging in price from 38,000 to 380,000 rupees, many families quietly walk out of the doctor’s consulting room upon hearing the estimated cost of treatment.

Studies by the Public Health Foundation of India show that spending on healthcare pushes about 55 million Indians a year below the poverty line .

Few Indians can afford the premiums for comprehensive health insurance. The government’s nationwide insurance scheme, Ayushman Bharat, covers treatment for some cancers but it provides only 500,000 rupees’ worth of annual cover for a family – the cost of just one dose of Kadcyla (ado-trastuzumab emtansine), a drug used to treat breast cancer. Patients may need up to 14 doses.

Dr Ravi Kannan is a surgical oncologist and director of Cachar cancer hospital and research centre in Silchar, Assam. He has worked in hospitals elsewhere in India and is familiar with doctors’ trauma of seeing patients walk out to go home and die.

“Some families start the treatment, hoping against hope to manage the cost. They start but they don’t come back for chemotherapy or radiation. They can’t sustain the cost,” he said. “The decision is a welcome step if the outcome is that more patients can access the drugs they need.”

India records about 1.56m new cancer cases annually – up from 1.39m cases in 2020 – making it a significant public health challenge.

As the supreme court delves deeper into the subject, what was clear, said Jyotsna Singh, co-convener of the Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatments, a civil society network, was that a “total overhaul” of the healthcare system was needed.

“Right from the cost of manufacturing a drug to the point of sale, we need to make the system transparent and regulate the entire supply chain. Only then will these drugs become available to those who need them,” she said.

Singh said companies and hospitals were likely to try to find legal loopholes to wriggle out of the 30% cap, suggesting that hospitals may offset the lower price charged for a drug by raising charges on other items.

The supreme court judges have also asked the government’s lawyers why the cap should apply only to cancer drugs and not the entire range of non-patented drugs. The court has given the government until 27 October to respond.

Unfortunately, the court’s ruling came too late for Radhakrishnan, who died in September 2022 while her case was still pending in Kerala.

title: Lights will stay on this winter, grid operator says after concerns
text:
The body in charge of Britain's electricity network has given assurances that the lights will stay on this winter after concerns were raised by some of its engineers.

The National Energy System Operator (NESO) said the country's electricity system was prepared and "resilient to the challenges it may face" during the colder months.

However, its winter outlook report comes after an independent investigation found engineers had "high levels of stress and concern" about their ability to ensure adequate supply due to differences between renewable and gas-fired power generation.

NESO said supplies were expected to remain secure throughout the winter, though warned there could be "tight days".

It added that such days would result in it deploying notices to power producers that additional electricity generation may be needed. It said such an announcement was not a warning of power cuts and was routine.

"While we never take resilience for granted, households and businesses can be confident that Great Britain's electricity system remains secure, reliable and among the most resilient in the world," said Deborah Petterson, director of whole energy system resilience at NESO.

In a separate report, National Gas, a private company that owns and runs the country's gas network, and is separate from NESO, said it expected to have sufficient supply to meet demand this winter, but forecast gas for power generation to increase at peak demand due to the "intermittent" nature of renewables.

The release of the two reports comes as Britain's energy generation and security falls under increasing scrutiny, given the wars in the Middle East and eastern Europe have pushed prices up and sparked supply fears.

The country's electricity is generated from a wide range of sources, including renewables such as solar and wind, as well as more traditional gas-fired and nuclear power stations.

Wind power was the largest generator of electricity in Britain last year, accounting for almost 30% of all power, marginally above gas.

However, there appear to be challenges in the transition to renewables in ensuring supply keeps up with demand, according to findings from an investigation into practices at NESO, which was commissioned following allegations over operational decision making and record keeping at the grid operator.

Law firm Eversheds Sutherland, which carried out the independent investigation, said there were "high levels of stress and concern" within NESO's Electricity National Control Centre over the "current state of the energy industry generally" and the longer-term ability to keep it balanced.

It said this was, according to evidence gathered from staff, due to the fact that traditional methods of electricity generation such as gas were "easier to manage", compared to renewables, which were "less flexible", and were making the job of ensuring supply meets demand "more difficult".

The probe also found there to be a "significant disconnect" between those working in the control room and NESO's leadership.

Multiple witnesses expressed the view that those in senior leadership and executive positions "do not fully appreciate or understand either the way in which the control room works, or the reality of the pressures faced by those on the frontline who are responsible for 'keeping the lights on'", Eversheds' report said.

The investigation was prompted after Conservative shadow energy secretary Clare Coutinho said in July she had been contacted by a whistle-blower alleging that NESO had been "hiding information about how securely our grid is being run".

One of the claims was that control room staff were encouraged to conceal or alter records to avoid leaving a paper trail linked to efforts to stabilise the grid during a period of extreme heat in June.

This was done in order for NESO, which is owned by the government, to avoid public scrutiny or reputational damage, according to the allegation.

Eversheds said its investigation did not substantiate any of the allegations from whistle-blowers but did identify "cultural, governance and control issues" that it said were "significant findings in their own right".

Fintan Slye, chief executive of NESO, said the investigation identified "areas where we could improve how colleagues can raise concerns and how we respond to them".

"I want all colleagues at NESO to feel heard. We will act on the recommendations, working closely with our trade unions, and be open with colleagues about the progress we make," he added.

title: ‘We’ve lost a basic sense of politeness’: UK readers reveal daily reality of public transport
author: Alfie Packham and Guardian readers
text:
Regular users detail their frustrations – and question whether Andy Burnham’s crackdown on antisocial behaviour will actually work

Andy Burnham has announced a campaign against nuisance behaviour on public transport, including “headphone dodgers” who play loud music .

“We’ve all been on the train when someone starts blasting music or videos from their phone,” Burnham said in a statement. “It gets on your nerves and can quickly spoil the journey.”

Six people share their views on Burnham’s new campaign and recount their experiences of antisocial behaviour on public transport.

I live in London and commute daily on the tube. Even yesterday, sitting next to me was a guy playing videos out loud, which is the most common issue. I’m interested in what has caused a sudden change to our social contract that allows people the psychological safety to completely disregard others. It’s not top of the list of worst behaviour; it’s in the same bracket as leaning on poles so no one can hold them, leaving your bag on the only seat left, leaning your arm on the fold up chair, or man-spreading. It mostly saddens me that we have lost a basic sense of politeness.

I’m not sure Andy Burnham’s announcement will do anything. If you’re already playing very loud videos in public, presumably you don’t care very much about what you should be doing. You never really see police or “safety officers”, so who would enforce it? I’m glad they aren’t making the tube workers or bus drivers try to enforce it though; it would make their days hell. Claire, 41, London

I get the train five nights a week to work and nine times out of 10, there is somebody taking phone calls on speakerphone, blasting videos or music, even in the so-called quiet carriage. Everyone’s too scared to ask them to move to a different carriage or turn it down, so it’s a regular occurrence. It makes my journey a nightmare. No one enforces anything. I doubt this new law will change this. It should include phone calls too and people putting calls on loudspeaker. It doesn’t go far enough. Margaret, 49, Weston-super-Mare

I think this is a great step to protect public spaces as shared spaces, and to show people the boundaries between acceptable and unacceptable behaviour. The last time I asked somebody who was playing reels aloud to use their headphones I was called “a piece of shit” and decided not to ask anybody that again. But commuters shouldn’t have to put up with it. Of course, the question is whether and how this will be enforced consistently. Ben Ellis, 38, Edinburgh

I’ve always challenged this behaviour by asking people if they have headphones. If they say no, I ask if they can turn the sound off. Most of the time this is OK, but I have had repeated incidents where people refuse. I’m stubborn and confident, so I’ll explain that it is not normal or socially acceptable to subject other people to jarring video scrolling. Only once in this situation did a train guard ask someone playing football at full volume to turn it off. And I can’t blame them. You’d be arguing with idiots for 90% of your shift if you did.

I’m sick of being the bad guy who points it out. It seems like people of all ages have forgotten basic decency and consideration. I had a run-in with a teenage kid who was watching TikTok or something, and he said, “What do you mean? If you were watching Netflix on your phone, wouldn’t you have the volume on?” So there’s a range of understanding of what people think is appropriate behaviour in a public place. John, 43, Sheffield

One of the bigger issues that never gets addressed is football fans on public transport. I’m a football fan myself, but fans on trains can be extremely offensive, oppressive, aggressive and difficult for people to deal with. One time that springs to mind was a bunch of fans on a two-carriage train. They were drinking, singing loud, offensive songs regardless of the fact that there were kids on the train, banging on the ceiling of the carriage, making a hell of a racket. There were no police or staff. There was a bunch of people waiting at the railway station at the other end, but it’s too late at that point.

It’s become almost like an accepted thing that if you go in on a train, this is what you have to put up with. I’m glad to see that [Burnham] recognises that behaviour on public transport is an issue that needs to be addressed. Do I think this will address it? Not at all. How do you get to someone on a train? Will this be app based? Only instant reporting and action will work, but how does that square with a public transport network with significant coverage gaps? Mike Hughes, 63, Tyldesley, Greater Manchester

The Manchester Metrolink has no [regular] conductors, so antisocial behaviour goes unchecked. It happens to the extent that it deters me from travelling on buses and trams. Trains aren’t quite as bad, because if someone’s really annoying, one can leave one’s seat to go and seek out the train manager and tell them what seat the offender is sitting in. This is impossible on the Manchester trams, so what possible incentive do habitual offenders have to desist? I suppose, over time, the campaign might lead to gradual social change – so even just raising and highlighting the issues might result in attitudinal change. My main concern is that it’s going to be nigh on useless having a fining policy unless transport is policed. It’ll end up like the law against hogging the middle lane on the motorway. How many people have been pulled up and fined for that? How many people still do it? Linda, Manchester

title: Have Man Utd become the unmanageable club?
text:
The cycle of doom that has ultimately engulfed every Manchester United manager since Sir Alex Ferguson now has the hapless Michael Carrick in its unforgiving grip.

Carrick recreated a familiar scene - the same one acted out by predecessor Ole Gunnar Solskjaer after a 4-1 loss at Watford in November 2021 cost him his job - by raising his hands in apology to supporters who had just seen United humiliated by the same scoreline at Como in the Champions League.

Carrick is the seventh full-time manager since Ferguson stepped down in 2013 after winning 38 trophies during 26 years in charge.

Since then there have been days of success under Louis van Gaal, Jose Mourinho and Erik ten Hag, and moments of hope, but the final outcome is always the same - dismissal.

Carrick will need something miraculous to change that storyline, with results poor and revolt within the dressing room as defender Lisandro Martinez took aim at director of football Jason Wilcox after the Champions League defeat at Atletico Madrid, while captain Bruno Fernandes questioned the tactics in Como.

It hints at something rotten in the state of United.

So should it really be crestfallen managers standing in front of those disappointed supporters?

Can it really be United's managers every time? Should not even more scrutiny now be aimed at those who appointed them, then decided the direction of the club?

Have United effectively, through years of decay, decline and appalling decision-making, become the unmanageable club?

There have been those seven full-time managers - David Moyes, Van Gaal, Mourinho, Solskjaer, Ten Hag, Ruben Amorim and Carrick. There have also been spells as interims for others such as Ryan Giggs, Ralf Rangnick, Ruud van Nistelrooy and Darren Fletcher.

United's leaders, from former executive vice-chairman Ed Woodward to the ruling Glazer family and now part-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe, have effectively tried every trick in the book to recreate the Ferguson era.

Moyes, an ill-starred appointment led by Ferguson, found the job too big for him after leaving Everton . Van Gaal and Mourinho were tried and trusted operators with stellar track records of success at Europe's superpowers. Solskjaer was effectively the anti-Mourinho without any sort of managerial track record that suggested he would succeed at United, but appointed after a successful spell in temporary charge.

Ten Hag got the job on the back of leading a superb young Ajax side to the Champions League semi-final. Amorim was regarded as European coaching's hottest young property when he was lured from Sporting in Lisbon.

All ended up sacked. All eventually found the unwieldy beast that is United impossible to tame.

Van Gaal won the FA Cup in 2016. Mourinho won the League Cup and the Europa League in 2017. Ten Hag won the FA Cup in 2024 with a landmark win against Manchester City .

Slim pickings compared to previous glories.

United, however, have not become a bad or dysfunctional club overnight. They have been heading towards this point ever since the succession plan to Ferguson - not easy, admittedly - was botched so badly.

Carlo Ancelotti, Pep Guardiola and Jurgen Klopp all felt able to resist the lure of Old Trafford, leading to what should have been red faces all round in December 2019, when they were all managing within 35 miles of each other in the north-west but none were at United.

Ancelotti was at Everton , Guardiola was at Manchester City . Klopp was at Liverpool . United had Solskjaer, an over-sentimental choice made on the back of a feelgood interim spell. He lasted less than three years.

With every passing day, Carrick looks like Solskjaer Mark II.

Carrick is a former fan favourite who did well in temporary charge, but whose previous managerial career was a sacking at Championship club Middlesbrough. Solskjaer shared that same unwanted distinction, sacked by Cardiff City in September 2014 after only nine months in charge as they struggled in the Championship.

It has all brought United to the point where the question must be asked. Since Ferguson's departure, has it ever been worse than it is now? In recent times, has there ever been less hope than there is now? Has morale ever been lower than it is now?

United will always find a manager should they require one, but their current parlous circumstances mean they are no longer the attraction they once were.

They will not have the pick of the globe's finest. They will need to persuade someone that there is a future at Old Trafford that contains something other than future dismissal, a sobering state of affairs for the self-styled "biggest club in the world".

Given the current state of United's squad, there is no guarantee a manager with a high-class track record would have a quick fix, or any fix at all, without huge investment.

Carrick is front of house and, on current evidence, will pay the price for United's failings. He is a repeat of the Solskjaer mistake, an easy choice made after taking them back into the Champions League, a comfort blanket with supporters that has now been torn away by poor results.

There are significant culprits elsewhere, led by Ratcliffe.

United fans have held regular protests against the Glazers since they took control in 2005, their leveraged purchase loading debt on to the club. They have remained majority owners, despite the level of angered aimed towards them from supporters, unmoved by years of ill feeling.

In turn, Ratcliffe's move into part-ownership alongside the Glazer family has meant fans turned on him for his association and business partnership with the hugely unpopular Americans.

Ratcliffe, like other successful billionaires before him, has found running a football club is a different world to the one he inhabited previously.

He has suggested he leaves big footballing decisions to others, such as Wilcox and chief executive Omar Berrada, but instability and rank bad decisions have come with Ratcliffe as United's leading figure.…

Britain’s gas security needs reinforcement. Last-minute deals with Belgium are not a proper fix
author: Nils Pratley
text:
The UK still imports 60% of its gas and, even with Jackdaw, its energy supply and resilience problems are not going away

A fter the overdue approval of the Jackdaw field in the North Sea, here comes a reminder that Britain still imports almost 60% of its gas and the stuff has to come from somewhere. We’re now doing a deal with Belgium to ensure enough supply can flow through a connecting pipeline this winter should a “low-probability but high-impact stress event”, to quote the regulatory mouthful, occur.

To be fair, the arrangement to maintain capacity from Belgium is a belt-and-braces measure. The imagined events do sound genuinely stressful and may never happen. A critical piece of infrastructure, such as the two import terminals in Milford Haven to bring in liquefied natural gas (LNG) into Britain, would have to be out of action during a prolonged cold snap in which demand is very high.

Equally, though, the “high-impact” bit matters: we’re talking about having enough supplies to run gas-fired power stations at full pelt if necessary to keep the lights on. You don’t take chances.

In short, 10p a month will be added to bills to cover the cost of paying Interconnector Limited, the Belgian owner of the pipeline, to maintain the compressors needed to shove big volumes of gas to Britain in a hurry if required. Without the arrangement, the company had already warned it would cut capacity, in part because the big pipe was not used much in practice last year.

The first conclusion – the comforting one – is that the deal sounds like decent value for money. As insurance policies go, £1.19 a household a year is not much.

The second, however, is that risks to Britain’s gas security are plainly mounting. The Ofgem document describing the Belgian deal says it was “the only currently available intervention identified that both addresses the immediate security of supply position for winter 2026/27 and provides continuing security of supply benefits over the following four years”. It was Belgium, plus any future deal on the Dutch pipeline, or nothing.

Nor is the Belgian shuffle a cure-all. “The agreement does not remove the need for further measures led by government that are likely to be required to support security of supply and wider gas system resilience over the medium and longer term,” says Ofgem.

The government should take that line as a heavy hint to get a move on. Do we need more gas storage, more LNG terminals, or both? And post-Jackdaw, what’s a realistic appraisal of how much will be sourced from the North Sea?

It is now almost a year since an alarming report from the National Energy System Operator (Neso) warned of an “emerging risk to gas supply security” in 2030. The government promised to “do whatever it takes” to avert a crunch but one cannot say it has actually done much. An interim response to the Neso report came in August but no timetable was given for choosing what kit or arrangements were needed and by when. The final response isn’t due until next year.

Read the “winter outlook” report from National Gas, published on Friday, and a few points stand out. Yes, it’s good news that, with the help of the Belgian deal, this winter’s outlook is positive. But the company also says that, even as annual consumption drifts down slightly, the peaks for demand remain as high as ever, driven by the role of gas-fired power generation when renewables output is low.

Like Ofgem, National Gas says “continued progress on government plans to reform security of supply arrangements will be vital to address enduring challenges in the years ahead”. It is becoming a theme.

The obvious answer is more gas storage to address Britain’s skimpy current levels. That could mean Centrica’s Rough facility in North Sea (currently due to close next spring), the Bains development led by dCarbonX off the north-west coast of England (which may happen anyway), more on-shore salt caverns or any combination. Or, perhaps, German-style forward-buying deals on LNG.

But something has to happen soon. None of this infrastructure gets built quickly and that 2030 potential crunch is getting closer. Certainly, the government cannot agonise for as long as it did over Jackdaw. Eleventh-hour deals with Belgium are not a permanent fix for Britain’s gas security headache.

title: Imagine if, for once, Labour decided to tell the truth about immigration | Gaby Hinsliff
author: Gaby Hinsliff
text:
Our economy needs it. The NHS needs it. And making foreign workers’ lives more miserable – as the home secretary plans to do – will undermine integration

My mum’s carer was uncharacteristically late one morning. She didn’t want to say why at first, but it turned out she’d found her previous client – an elderly lady living all alone, with no family to visit – collapsed on the floor, barely alive. It was a lot to cope with for someone only in their early 20s, a reminder of the heavy responsibility this job carries. Watching the carers who helped both my parents in their respective final weeks taught me that while the work itself might seem mundane, the emotional and social skills needed to do it well – to coax some sense out of the confused, to jolly along the lonely, and to soothe the dying, to walk in and out of unfamiliar houses all day long without quite knowing what you might find – are anything but.

Yet like so many jobs predominantly done by women, care has long been relentlessly undervalued. That means lousy pay, little public recognition, and now – at least for the disproportionately large chunk of this workforce who are migrant workers – the disorientating realisation that the government can snap its fingers and all your life plans are upended overnight.

Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

title: Jim Chalmers faces a world of hard choices where the solution to one problem makes the other worse
author: Patrick Commins
text:
High inflation, low growth and rising unemployment can be added to the federal treasurer’s wall of worries

Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast

Jim Chalmers in a speech last week offered the scant encouragement that the economy would be “a bit better” in a year’s time.

Fast forward to Friday morning, and the treasurer revealed that his officials were busy downgrading their forecasts ahead of December’s mid-year budget update to show slower growth and higher unemployment.

In other words, things are getting worse, not better.

Overnight, a broadening Middle East conflict pushed the global benchmark oil price to US$113, and within sight of its April high of nearly US$120.

Motorists are paying 60 cents more for a litre of petrol prices than they were before the US and Israel attacked Iran. That’s an extra $36 to fill up a 60-litre tank. Do that once a week and a family’s monthly fuel bill is $144 higher than in February.

The New York Times overnight reported that the US and Israel have drawn up plans to restart attacks on Iran after the upcoming American midterm elections.

Westpac analysts have sketched out an “escalation” scenario for the Middle East conflict where oil climbs towards US$150, echoing warnings from the International Monetary Fund earlier this month.

That worst-case scenario would have huge implications for inflation and interest rates, even as we brace for a potential fifth interest rate hike on 3 November.

Meanwhile, the one bright spot that has helped paper over many of the cracks in the global economy – the huge spending associated with artificial intelligence – has hit some serious wobbles .

Investors are worried about the huge surge in debt among companies racing to build the infrastructure for an AI future – the trigger for another steep sell-off on Wall Street overnight.

Community opposition to the massive datacentre build-out could stall the headlong rush towards an AI future. That is likely a good thing in the longer term, but in the short term is another stress to add to the wall of worries. Rising chatter of a new tech stock bubble is naturally accompanied by talk of an imminent bust.

With all this going on, no wonder that the treasurer can only offer the thinnest of gruel for Australians hungry for any evidence of an end to years of disruption, and of wages that can’t keep up with high and rising prices.

High inflation, low growth and rising unemployment is a central banker’s “nightmare”, as the Reserve Bank’s Andrew Hauser has said.

It’s also a nightmare for a federal treasurer who is increasingly unpopular and desperate for a win in the court of public opinion.

“The pressures on people right now are very substantial and obviously that keeps me awake at night,” Chalmers told Politico.

“And there’s a number of reasons for that, some of them are outside our control, and some of them we have some influence over. You know, providing some cost-of-living help, managing the budget in a responsible way,” he said.

“Those are the things that we can do, but in lots of ways we’re hostage as well to decisions taken in DC or Tehran or in Eastern Europe about two wars which are pushing up inflation around the world and weighing on growth around the world.”

The high level of government spending is not helping the inflation fight, by any means – something the opposition is keen to point out at every opportunity.

Productivity growth is, if not dead, then resting, and shows no signs of springing back to its perch. That means more inflation at lower rates of growth as the economy hits its speed limits sooner.

But Chalmers is right when he says there’s a lot that is out of the government’s control.

His options to alleviate voter discontent are limited, which is why he frequently falls back on platitudes and lines to the effect of “you think we have it bad? You should see other economies.”

Sure, the government can lower petrol prices through another temporary cut to the fuel excise. But the billions of dollars that pumps into motorists’ pockets makes it harder for the RBA to bring inflation back under control.

Labor could go the other way and announce plans for big spending cuts in the December mid-year economic and fiscal outlook.

That would help the central bank’s job, but would drag on an already weak economy and push unemployment higher – would they win any plaudits for that?

This is Hauser’s “world of hard choices” – a world where the solution to one problem makes the other worse. A world with which Australians are becoming all too familiar.

title: Game Preview: Knicks at Celtics, October 23, 2026
author: Moritz Wollert
text:
The Knicks meet Mitchell Robinson for Boston’s home opener

Remember the good old days of just caring about diamond rings, roughly 70 square feet of fabric and the feelings of Ariel Hukporti? Yeah, me neither. It’s what a loss against the Philadelphia 76ers on Banner Night at Madison Square Garden can do to you. It functions as a stark reminder that the new NBA season is upon us and the Knicks somehow have to find a way to let the past be the past and kick some serious you-know-what in the present. On Friday night in Boston, though, it will once again be hard to keep the nostalgia at bay. Even if Mitchell Robinson is not wearing the orange and blue anymore.

The former longest-tenured Knick has moved on to (not so) greener pastures and now starts for one of New York’s biggest rivals a good 200 miles up north. There’s probably no Knicks fan out there who won’t have some weird feeling in their stomach seeing the “Blockness Monster” in a uniform we’ve all been brought up to hate. And if I had to guess, I’d bet that Mr. Robinson puts in quite an effort on the glass tonight. Maybe Mitch even offers a glimpse of an expanded “bag,” as people like to call it these days. He’ll want to show his former team what they’re missing without him and prove to the Land of the Leprechauns that the $48 million they left for him at the end of the free agency rainbow wasn’t fool’s gold.

In Boston’s season opener, Mitch did not make a great impression on the C’s fanbase. Outside of Paul George, though, few players in green and white did. The Celtics lost at Detroit despite leading by 22 four minutes into the third quarter and by 10 with eight minutes left in the fourth. Somehow, someway, that sounds familiar, doesn’t it? And the Boston Celtics haven’t really changed that much from that incredibly entertaining playoff series they played with your beloved Bockers 17 months ago. Their personnel certainly changed, but in terms of their style of play, it’s still bombs away in Beantown.

Boston’s barrage of threes can overwhelm an opponent, just as it did against the Pistons for roughly three quarters on Tuesday, when the Celtics attempted 42 shots from downtown. Their shooting creates a lot of space to operate, puts a lot of stress on the opposing defense and can turn any game in an instant. That cuts both ways, though, because the Celtics really don’t care if they are up by 20 or down by 20. They just keep shooting, and sometimes they shoot themselves in the foot. They certainly did at Detroit, where they let a shell-shocked Pistons team right back into the game with quick shots, nonexistent floor balance and bad transition defense.

The latter part of that contest was especially ugly for Boston, as they allowed 39 points in the final quarter. Their lone remaining superstar, Jayson Tatum, had an awful shooting performance and could not steady his teammates. He missed 17 of his 23 shots and did not provide the much-needed dimension his isolation scoring usually gives Boston from the top of the key. After Jaylen Brown was traded to Philadelphia, the Celtics really do not have that many guys who are comfortable creating their own shot. If Tatum isn’t performing at the All-NBA level he reached before his gruesome Achilles injury, it could become a problem all season long.

The one big bright spot for Boston was the play of Paul George, who looked like he wanted to turn back the clock to his old Pacer days. His 38 points were the most ever scored by a Celtic in his debut, and he only needed 21 shots to do it. Not many Bostonians were especially excited to subscribe to the Podcast P experience, but this performance eased at least a few of their worries. Joe Mazzulla’s shot-happy system should suit George quite a bit, and maybe he surprises a lot of people with a solid year.

Besides their two big-name wings, Boston will look to Derrick White and Payton Pritchard to provide most of the scoring. White struggled from the floor in Boston’s first-round playoff loss last season, shooting 32.1 percent, while Pritchard remains one of the elite bench energizers in the entire league. The rest of the Celtics’ rotation includes their three centers, Mitch, Luka Garza and Neemias Queta; a bevy of scrappy younger guys like Hugo Gonzalez, Baylor Scheierman and Jordan Walsh; and elite marksman Sam Hauser. Rookie big Chris Cenac, Mike Conley (yes, he’s still around) and Ron Harper Jr. did not see any action versus Detroit.

Not exactly the scariest bunch on paper, right? Make no mistake, Boston has made a habit of getting consistent results from Mazzulla’s system. They run a professional organization, have a system that more often than not works like a well-oiled machine and have a clear plan for beating their opponent. Tatum is one of the best players in the NBA and surely wants to remind Boston fans that he was the right All-Star wing to build around. So expect a big effort out of him, Mitch and the rest of the Celtics.

For New York, defending the arc and finishing possessions on the glass will be essential, especially with Mitch hunting second chances. Boston’s collapse in Detroit also showed why the Knicks should look to push after misses and take advantage before the Celtics can set their defense. Whatever they throw at New York on Friday won’t surprise our veteran-laden Knickerbockers. But walking into Boston for its home opener and handing the Celtics a second consecutive loss will still be a tall order.

Of course, that’s exactly what we hope to remember from this game. So let’s go Knicks!

Who: New York Knicks (0-1) at Boston Celtics (0-1) Date: Friday, October 23, 2026 Time: 7:00 PM ET Place: TD Garden, Boston, MA TV: Prime Video Follow: @ptknicksblog (X) and @postingandtoasting (BlueSky)

Devin Carter will miss the game for the Celtics with mononucleosis. As of this writing, nothing of note for the Knicks.

title: Brazil’s election and the battle for the Amazon – podcast
author: Presented by Helen Pidd with Tom Phillips; produced by Ivor Manley, Eli Block and Ross Burns; executive producer Sami Kent
text:

For the Amazon and the communities who live there, the stakes in Sunday’s Brazilian presidential election runoff could scarcely be higher.

Our Latin America correspondent, Tom Phillips heads to Roraima, the country’s most northern state, to hear from voters, preachers and politicians in a region that heavily backed Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round.

He finds them all hopeful that the far-right candidate will bring back the mining that his father Jair so heartily encouraged when in power in an administration that oversaw the felling of 11m acres (4.5m hectares) of rainforest.

Tom also meets Indigenous activists determined to fight back even if the Bolsonaros take power again.

Helen Pidd asks what it will all mean, not only for Brazil but also for the climate crisis more broadly.
